words.why: It is a headword in the academies' dictionary with exactly the standards meaning ("que fija la norma"). Standards bodies in Spain (UNE), Mexico (NMX-Z-013) and Mercosur (AMN), and the Spanish W3C WCAG 2.0, all use it for the binding parts of a standard. Philosophy uses it the same way ("ética normativa"). I re-read every one of these on the page.
words.spelling_on_plaque: NORMATIVO. No accent, masculine singular. Do not use NORMATIVA alone: the dictionary lists the feminine as a noun meaning a body of rules.
words.competing_forms: None for this sense. (OBLIGATORIO / PRECEPTIVO are near-synonyms in the dictionary but are not the standards-writing term.)
words.regions: Confirmed in sources from Spain, Mexico, Colombia, Argentina/Mercosur. No regional variation found.

words.why: The phrase exists and is not invented: it is the plain opposite of 'normativo' in law, philosophy and the W3C tradition, always two words with no hyphen. The note: the standards bodies I could read (UNE, NMX, AMN) never use it. Their label for the non-binding parts is INFORMATIVO, and W3C's Spanish glossary gives 'no normativo' only as a synonym of 'informativo'. So NO NORMATIVO is correct Spanish and keeps the visible pairing with NORMATIVO, but a standards writer would expect INFORMATIVO on an annex. Which one goes on the plaque is Carey's choice between two real forms.
words.spelling_on_plaque: NO NORMATIVO: two words, no hyphen, no accent, masculine singular. The Diccionario panhispánico de dudas rules this directly. NO-NORMATIVO and NONORMATIVO are wrong.
words.competing_forms: INFORMATIVO is the official standards label (UNE, NMX-Z-013, AMN, and the headword in the Spanish WCAG 2.0 glossary). It matches the project's own table ('Informative / Advisory'). It loses the visible NORMATIVO / NO NORMATIVO pairing.
words.regions: 'No normativo' confirmed in texts from Spain, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia. 'Informativo' confirmed in Spain, Mexico and Mercosur standards. No regional split found.

words.why: CRÍTICO is the exact, established Spanish counterpart of English 'critical', with the same range of meanings and the same Greek root (krinein): judging ('pensamiento crítico', 'Teoría Crítica') and grave/decisive ('estado crítico', 'periodo crítico'). The note: no Spanish dictionary sense or standards text uses it to mean 'inverts the standard' or 'MUST NOT'. That meaning is the project's own, in Spanish exactly as in English, so the translation is faithful but the plaque sense is not something Spanish already has. Standing alone, a Spanish reader will most likely read it as 'grave condition' (the dictionary's own example is 'Estado crítico del herido') or 'given to criticism'.
words.spelling_on_plaque: CRÍTICO, with the accent on the first I. The accent is obligatory in capitals; CRITICO is a spelling error. Masculine singular.
words.competing_forms: None that is an established one-word equivalent. Spanish RFC 2119 translations render MUST NOT as NO DEBE, not with any adjective. PROHIBIDO would say 'forbidden' but is not a translation of CRITICAL.
words.regions: Confirmed in Spain (dictionary, nursing journal), Mexico, Colombia, Costa Rica. Same senses everywhere.

words.why: It is the standard form in Spanish-language psychology and education for Flavell's concept, confirmed in papers from Chile, Spain and Colombia, and it outnumbers the older variant on Dialnet by 3.277 documents to 19. The note: it is not an entry in the academies' dictionary (nor are metacognición or metacognoscitivo), so its standing rests on scholarly use, not on a dictionary ruling. It is regularly formed from two dictionary entries (meta- 'acerca de' + cognitivo) and appears on an ASALE page in a talk title. The project's sense ('the observer audits the frame') is a little wider than the psychology sense ('thinking about one's own thinking'), in Spanish as in English.

quotes_altered_or_not_found: No quotation was altered or missing: all 52 were found on the pages as quoted. Minor notes follow on things around the quotes.
DLE 'crítico' and DLE 'no': the sweep's quotes are faithful but selective (the crítico quote skips sense 2 'relativo a la crisis'; the 'no' quote drops the last example, 'No muy lejos de allí').
AMN Directivas definition 3.10: wording confirmed, but the PDF is a two-column Spanish/Portuguese layout, so the Spanish sentence is interleaved with Portuguese in the extracted text.

COUNT NOT REPRODUCED - NMX-Z-013: the sweep reported 120 hits for 'normativ' and 43 for 'informativ'. My full-text read gave 62 and 42. The figure that matters, 0 hits for 'no normativ', I did reproduce.

COUNT NOT REPRODUCED - UNE-EN 301549: the sweep said 30 '(Informativo)' labels. I counted 8 '(Informativo)' and 2 '(Normativo)' in my extraction. I did reproduce 44 hits for 'informativ-' and 0 for 'no normativo/a', 'no es normativ-', 'no son normativ-'.

Sweep 2 claim 'the Mexican standard sets normativo against informativo (en oposición al normativo)': confirmed, the phrase is in 6.4.1.1 and mirrored in the normative-annex clause ('en oposición al informativo').

Sweep 3 said it could not tell whether the Mexican 2017 article (Berridi) also uses 'metacognitivo'. It does: I found 'capacidades metacognitivas' in the body, alongside three 'metacognoscitiv-' forms.
Sweep 2 could not confirm the sentence 'Esta sección no es normativa' in the Colombian MOTA specification. I found it twice in the file (sections 1 and 2).

Sweep 1 read only the opening of the Fundéu 'no + sustantivo' page. I read the body: it says the construction 'se ha censurado en ocasiones por considerarse anglicismo' and then rejects that objection, citing the Nueva gramática.

Small attribution points: the Osses/Jaramillo authors are at Universidad de La Frontera (Temuco); the journal is published by Universidad Austral de Chile. The Index de Enfermería article (Granada journal) appears to be by an author based in Chile, so it is weaker as evidence of usage 'in Spain'.

Method note: three DPD/PDF quotes (DPD 'tilde', DPD 'concordancia', the Universidad de Flores article) were confirmed through the scraper's direct-quote extraction of the opened page, not by my own reading of the raw text. The three standards PDFs (UNE, NMX, AMN) were read as text streamed from the PDF, nothing saved to disk.

for_a_native_expert: NO NORMATIVO or INFORMATIVO on the second plaque: both are real. Which one would a Spanish-speaking standards editor or philosopher of norms expect to see next to NORMATIVO on an object like this?

How CRÍTICO reads alone on a medallion beside NORMATIVO: as 'grave condition', as 'given to criticism', or as the intended 'opposes the norm'? This is a question of first impression that sources cannot settle.
Whether METACOGNITIVO, a psychology term, reads naturally to a philosopher for 'the observer audits the frame', or whether it sounds narrowly like classroom learning strategies.
Whether four bare masculine adjectives with no noun (implied 'estado') feel natural as labels, or whether a reader expects a noun or a different gender.
Whether any country's readers would find METACOGNOSCITIVO more correct (the sources say no, but only the Mexican variant was seen in live use).
verdict.plain_summary:
I re-opened every quoted page: all 52 quotations are there as quoted, and nothing had to be dropped. Two word counts from the standards sweep did not reproduce, but the count that matters did: "no normativo" appears zero times in the Spanish and Mexican standards.

All four Spanish words already exist, and nothing needs to be invented. The spellings proposed are right.

- **NORMATIVO**: established. It is in the academies' dictionary with the standards meaning, and Spain, Mexico and Mercosur standards bodies use it.
- **NO NORMATIVO**: established, with a note. It is correct Spanish, two words with no hyphen, and is used in law, philosophy and the Spanish W3C text. But the standards bodies' own label for the non-binding parts is INFORMATIVO, which also matches your table ("Informative / Advisory").
- **CRÍTICO**: established as the exact counterpart of "critical", with a note. The accent is obligatory in capitals. No Spanish source uses it to mean "inverts the standard"; that meaning is the project's own, in Spanish as in English. Alone, it will most likely read as "grave" or "given to criticism".
- **METACOGNITIVO**: established in scholarship, with a note. It is not in the academies' dictionary, but it is the normal term in psychology and education and outnumbers the older "metacognoscitivo" by 3.277 to 19 on Dialnet. One solid word, no accent.

Masculine singular is the right form for all four, and they hold across Spain and Latin America in the sources read.

Decision for you: NO NORMATIVO or INFORMATIVO on the second plaque. NO NORMATIVO keeps the visible pairing with NORMATIVO, as the English does; INFORMATIVO is what a standards writer expects. I would keep NO NORMATIVO for the pairing, and a native-speaking reader is the right person to confirm that and to say how CRÍTICO reads on its own.

Not checked: the academies' usage-dictionary pages on cognitivo/cognoscitivo were down again, and no official Spanish ISO drafting rules or Colombian, Chilean, Peruvian or Argentine national rules were opened.

findings.claim: NORMATIVO is a full entry in the academies' dictionary (headword 'normativo, va'), as an adjective, with the standards sense: 'that sets the norm'. Synonyms listed include reglamentario and preceptivo.
findings.quote_es: 1. adj. Que fija la norma. 2. adj. Perteneciente o relativo a la norma.
findings.source: normativo, va | Diccionario de la lengua española (RAE-ASALE), versión electrónica 23.8.1

findings.claim: CRÍTICO is a full entry (headword 'crítico, ca'), written with an accent on the first i. Its adjective senses are 'relating to criticism', 'relating to crisis', 'very difficult or grave', and a physics sense of a threshold value. None of the senses says 'forbidden' or 'inverts the standard'; a Spanish reader will most likely read it as 'grave/critical state' or 'given to criticism'.

findings.claim: The Diccionario panhispánico de dudas rules directly on 'no' before nouns and adjectives: it is written as a separate word with no hyphen. Its own example is an adjective (actitud no beligerante). So the correct form is NO NORMATIVO, two words; not NO-NORMATIVO and not NONORMATIVO.

findings.claim: The main dictionary records this use of 'no' as a normal sense of the adverb, with an adjective example, and with no mark calling it an anglicism or incorrect.

The Fundéu page is about nouns; the adjective case is covered by the DPD entry above.

findings.claim: Gender and number: a Spanish adjective agrees with the noun it modifies. The noun the plaques imply, estado, is masculine in the dictionary ('1. m.'), so masculine singular (NORMATIVO, NO NORMATIVO, CRÍTICO, METACOGNITIVO) is the matching form. The dictionary also cites adjectives by their masculine form (normativo, va; crítico, ca). Note that NORMATIVA alone would be read as the feminine noun 'body of rules', a different meaning.

Any dictionary sense of crítico that matches the project's meaning 'this inverts the standard / MUST NOT'. The DLE senses are criticism, crisis, gravity, opportune moment, fault-finding, and a physics threshold.

The full body text of the Fundéu 'no + sustantivo' page did not render; I read only its opening passage from the page's description field. I did not open the full Ortografía 2010 chapter on prefixes directly; the prefix rule is quoted from FundéuRAE's summary of it.
sweeps.plain_summary:
Three of the four plaques are settled by the academies' own sources; the fourth is correctly formed but not in the dictionary.

- **NORMATIVO**: a dictionary entry with exactly the standards meaning ("que fija la norma"). Use as is.
- **NO NORMATIVO**: the Diccionario panhispánico de dudas rules that "no" before an adjective is written as a separate word with no hyphen. Two words is correct; NO-NORMATIVO and NONORMATIVO are not. The main dictionary lists this use of "no" without marking it as an anglicism.
- **CRÍTICO**: a dictionary entry, and the accent is obligatory in capitals (DPD, the Ortografía and FundéuRAE all say so). The spelling is right, but the meaning needs a decision: the dictionary senses are "relating to criticism" and "very grave" (its own example is "estado crítico del herido"). None means "forbidden" or "inverts the standard", so a Spanish reader may read it as "serious condition".
- **METACOGNITIVO**: not in the Diccionario de la lengua española, and neither are metacognición or metacognoscitivo. Its parts are both entries (meta- "acerca de" and cognitivo, va), prefixes are written joined, and the word appears in a talk title on an ASALE page. So it is one solid word, regularly formed, with no accent; whether it is the established term in psychology and philosophy is for the other two sweeps to confirm.

Masculine singular is the right form: adjectives agree with their noun, "estado" is masculine, and "normativa" alone would read as the noun "body of rules".

I found no RAE or Fundéu note about "metacognitivo" or about the phrase "no normativo". rae.es went down partway through (error 522), so I could not open the DPD entries for cognitivo/cognoscitivo or the Diccionario histórico page that appears to use "no normativo".

sweeps.plain_summary:
NORMATIVO is the established word in every standards source I could open. NO NORMATIVO is real and correctly spelled, but the standards bodies' own label for the non-binding parts is INFORMATIVO.

**Normativo.** Spain (UNE), Mercosur (AMN) and Mexico (NMX-Z-013) all use it for the binding parts of a standard: "elementos normativos", "anexo normativo", "Anexo C (Normativo)", "referencias normativas". The Spanish W3C WCAG 2.0 does the same ("Esta sección es normativa").

**No normativo.** The three standards bodies never use it:
- **UNE-EN 301549:2020 (Spain):** 0 occurrences of "no normativo/a" in the full text, against 44 of "informativ-".
- **NMX-Z-013 (Mexico):** 0 occurrences of "no normativ", against 43 of "informativ" and 120 of "normativ".
- **AMN (Mercosur):** elements are classed by "carácter normativo/informativo"; no "no normativo" in the text I saw.

It does exist in Spanish standards language in the W3C tradition. Both Spanish translations of WCAG 2.0 say, in the glossary: «El contenido identificado como "informativo" o "no normativo" no se considera obligatorio para la conformidad». A Colombian specification written in W3C style uses "no normativas / no normativos" as the section status. An Argentine university article glosses an IRAM annex as "anexo informativo no normativo".

**What this means for the plaque.** NO NORMATIVO is understood, and where it appears it is written as two words with no hyphen. It keeps the visible pairing with NORMATIVO, as the English NON-NORMATIVE does. INFORMATIVO is what a Spanish-speaking standards writer would expect on an annex, and it matches the project's own table ("Informative / Advisory"). That choice is Carey's; both forms exist and neither is invented.

**RFC 2119 context.** MUST / MUST NOT is DEBE / NO DEBE in all three Spanish sources I opened. The secondary keywords vary (OBLIGATORIO vs REQUERIDO, RECOMENDADO vs RECOMIENDA). None of this bears on the word "crítico", which this sweep did not find in standards usage. This sweep did not cover "metacognitivo" or the philosophical sense of "crítico".

**Main gaps.** I could not open an official Spanish text of the ISO/IEC Directives Part 2, UNE's own drafting guide, or any ICONTEC, INN, INACAL or IRAM drafting rules. W3C lists no authorized Spanish WCAG 2.1 or 2.2.

sweeps.plain_summary:
All four Spanish words already exist in Spanish-language scholarship, in the forms proposed, across Spain, Mexico, Colombia, Argentina, Chile and Costa Rica. Nothing needs to be invented.

METACOGNITIVO: this is the standard form today. Papers from Chile (2008), Spain (2013) and Colombia (2008, 2011) all use 'metacognición' and 'metacognitivo' for Flavell's concept. The older variant 'metacognoscitivo' is real and still appears, mainly in Mexican writing (one 2017 UNAM-journal article uses it throughout), but it is rare: Dialnet returns 3.277 documents for 'metacognitivo' against 19 for 'metacognoscitivo'. Use METACOGNITIVO.

NORMATIVO / NO NORMATIVO: 'no normativo' is an established partner word of 'normativo', written as two words with no hyphen in every source I opened. It appears as a fixed pair in law ('enunciados normativos y no normativos', Mexico/Argentina 2013), in psychology ('sucesos normativos y no normativos', Argentina 2006; Colombia 2002) and in a Spanish philosophy encyclopedia (2019, 2021). 'Ética normativa' is the standard name of a branch of ethics (Mexico 2013, Colombia 2023). One thing to know: in psychology the pair means 'expected' versus 'unexpected' life events, while in law and philosophy it means 'norm-stating' versus 'not norm-stating'. The second meaning is the one the project wants, and it is well attested.

CRÍTICO: correct and standard in 'pensamiento crítico' and 'teoría crítica' (Costa Rica 2014, Colombia 2003, Spain 2019). It also carries the 'grave / decisive moment' sense just as English does: 'estado crítico', 'paciente crítico', 'periodo crítico' (Mexico 2014, 2017; Bolivia 2022). A Mexican history-of-concepts article (2015) explains why: 'crítica' and 'crisis' both descend from Greek krinein. I found no Spanish source using 'crítico' to mean 'inverts the standard'; that meaning is the project's own, in Spanish as in English.
